locator.quote: The question is the smallest power that works uniformly over all total functions and all input lengths.

feedback.feedback: The opening postpones the first executable winning-column object while accumulating the uniform infimum, k-dependent family bounds, exact logarithms and coefficient, source reconstruction status, and a detailed route map. Section 2 then starts with the general column and the stopped-simulator estimate before instantiating the promised four-column board. In the PDF, that board first becomes executable on page 6. These statements are largely explained and correct; the remaining problem is the order in which they become useful.
feedback.why_it_matters: The declared novice must hold several scales and proof obligations before being able to point to one candidate and decide whether it wins. Later local clarifications do not remove that initial working-memory cost. The goal is to bring the construction earlier without depriving the reader of a precise result.
feedback.advice: Use the opening for the access model, total-versus-promised distinction, the question, source credit, and a short qualitative explanation of the two powers. Keep a clearly signposted exact theorem, but relocate its detailed family parameters to one named theorem at the end of the general supplier/construction interface in Section 3, before Section 4 uses its bounds. Keep m, r and S defined before the earlier symbolic local-test count; moving the family theorem does not postpone every parameter definition. In Section 2, instantiate the four-column fields and winning conditions before scaling to m,r,ell. Move the quantitative rationale for r=20 log2(m), including the stopped-simulator vocabulary at line 129, to the classical proof where the guessing event has been defined. Reuse the existing material; do not add another introductory overview.
available_before: The OR access example
Definitions of R,Q,error and worst-case cap
The distinction between total and partial functions
feedback.missing_bridge: The reader has not yet performed a certificate lookup or a winning-condition check when the exact scale hierarchy is introduced.

Questions 3 and 4 test two vital hypotheses; neither directly asks the learner to assemble the three charges into the claimed scale.
feedback.why_it_matters: The title promises an explanation of the exponent. A learner may finish the adaptive examples yet retain “planting plus a direct product” as a method name rather than being able to derive why a global budget is divided by mL and why address guessing has no extra factor m.
feedback.advice: After the first-difference inequality, insert a compact preview of the three charges, with events stated before formulas: erased selected zero, heavily queried selected address tuple, and a light true-cell visit at some time. Reuse this map at the final gap rather than adding a second overview. Add or retarget one short synthesis task: use the integer-compatible bound G<=c mL (or G=floor(c mL)), identify which terms are bounded using L<=m and r=20 log2(m), and explain why averaging a uniformly independent selected column cancels m. The worked answer should show these operations, not only repeat the final inequality. Retarget or extend the existing final combined task rather than add a redundant sixth exercise. Name these as upper-bound charges: they may overlap, and overcounting is permitted.
